speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister without Portfolio):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board; Minister Without Portfolio
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PAYMENTS FOR REDUCTION OF WHEAT ACREAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the carryover of wheat in Canada will be approximately 950 million bushels on July 31 of this year, equivalent to nearly two years' disappearance. To reach a stock position in reasonable relationship to normal sales volumes, production of wheat must be reduced substantially below sales level. The number of years during which production need be so reduced depends upon the vigour with which the problem is attacked.
Closely related to the surplus in wheat is a current shortage of cash among western grain growers. The effects of a cash shortage are evident throughout the Prairies, but are particularly acute in Saskatchewan whose farmers are now carrying more than two-thirds of the total stocks on farms.
Unless strong action is taken now the prospect is for a heavy movement of acreage out of wheat and into coarse grains and oilseeds. The wheat producer is in a position in which he must attempt to increase his cash return. In large measure, this would lead to increased acreage in other crops. Our stock positions, particularly in oats and barley, are already high. A further increase in acreage in these crops this year would result in burdensome surplus and lower prices for these products. This would create extreme difficulties for producers whose incomes normally depend on the sales of these crops.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
In oilseeds there is reason to believe that some increase can be accommodated without serious effects on prices and delivery levels

February 27, 1970
Grain Payments
available to producers. Indications are, however, that rapeseed acreages will be increased sharply this year to the point where surplus in this crop appears to be a likelihood.
We recognize that long-term adjustment programs are needed and the government is hard at work on these. In the meantime we are faced with a serious wheat surplus situation that must be relieved quickly if we hope to prevent this problem from seriously injuring the whole agricultural industry.
Producers on their own initiative reduced wheat plantings by five million acres in 1969. However, the current income and cash position of prairie grain producers makes it unrealistic to expect that producers would reduce plantings to a desirable level in 1970, bearing this further major adjustment without direct government assistance.
Government leadership is necessary if adjustment is to take place without creating more serious problems, not only for wheat farmers but for farmers throughout Canada, and by extension for the whole economy. Whatever government action is taken the weight of the adjustment must be borne by wheat producers themselves-and I believe they will accept the need to make the adjustment.
The government proposes to implement a program to reduce wheat acreage and to encourage farmers in the Wheat Board designated region to hold this land out of production of any crop this year. I have discussed this program fully with the leaders of farm organizations in western Canada and in many respects the program as it is now proposed has been improved by the adoption of their recommendations.
The proposed program is as follows:
Producers in the Wheat Board designated region who reduce wheat acreage below 1969 levels and increase summerfallow or perennial forage by the same amount will receive federal compensation payments of $6 per acre for additions to summerfallow or $10 per acre for additions to perennial forage acreage. Partial payment will be made before the end of July and the balance will be paid in the fall of this year.
Compensation payments will be available to a maximum of 22 million acres of additional summerfallow and 2 million acres of additional perennial forage. A maximum of 1,000 acres for any individual producer will be eligible for compensation payments.

The actual cost to the government of the program, which will be administered by the Canada Department of Agriculture, is estimated at $100 million.
Wheat delivery quotas for the 1970-71 crop year will be based on the total of
(a)	25 per cent of summerfallow acreage as stated on the producers 1969 permit book,
(b)	total acreage of summerfallow in 1970, and
(c)	the amount by which acreage in perennial forage in 1970 exceeds the acreage in perennial forage in 1969.
Quotas for oats, barley, soft spring wheat and other crops to which delivery quotas apply will be based on acres seeded to each crop in 1970. In addition, any producer may choose to allocate any or all of his acres qualified for wheat quota to any other crop instead of wheat.
This program will provide needed income to hard-pressed grain growers and encourage them to dispose of wheat stocks already piled up on their farms. It will allow farmers to cut back drastically on wheat acreage while at the same time discouraging the wholesale switch to other crops.
A sharp reduction in wheat stocks will greatly enhance the continuing effort to strengthen international wheat prices. Foreign buyers are not willing to pay top prices when they know we are sitting on a mountain of grain. If farmers get behind this program and support it to the fullest, as I am sure they will, the cash position of grain producers and the whole prairie economy will be substantially improved this fall.
This major initiative in reducing wheat stocks provides a unique opportunity for moving forward toward co-ordinated global programs of production policies for grain. The benefits from the new Canadian program will extend well beyond Canada to the world wheat economy. The governments of other exporting nations are similarly preoccupied with the problems of surplus production; some have programs in place or are examining new ones designed to minimize the problem. This initiative in Canada, which represents a new and much stronger attack on the problems of surplus production, should add impetus to international efforts to stabilize the world grain economy.
In order that this opportunity should not be lost, I have proposed to the governments of Australia, Argentina and the U.S.A. and to the Commission of the European Economic
February 27, 1970

Community that a meeting be held at ministerial level to review the Canadian program and consider complementary action which might be taken by others designed to compound its benefits internationally. I am confident these governments will agree to participate in an early meeting and I am hopeful this will mark a turning point in our efforts to rationalize the world grain situation.
In the meantime, every effort is being made to increase export sales. Increased food aid shipments and more attractive credit facilities have assisted the Canadian Wheat Board in attaining sales that will reach 375 million bushels this year, greater than any year save one in the history of the board from 1943 to the year of the first major purchase by the U.S.S.R. in 1963.
With the successful completion of this major reduction program, market forecasts indicate that Canada will be able to return to a level of production in the area of 20 million acres. Additional measures will be required in 1971 to assure that production does not exceed acceptable levels.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PAYMENTS FOR REDUCTION OF WHEAT ACREAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one thought was expressed by the minister with which I am in complete agreement, that this is a situation which requires government leadership. After listening to the minister we are still waiting for that leadership. The opposition has been pressing for months to get the government to make commitments as to its long-range intention with regard to agricultural problems, including the extremely serious situation in western Canada. As usual, we have been fobbed off by the minister and his colleague the Minister of Agriculture who hide behind the officially accepted phrase that the government uses to cover up inaction and incompetence and inefficiency-"The government has the matter under consideration and will announce its policy in due course."
The day of "due course" has arrived, Mr. Speaker. The minister has laboured and produced a limited and shabby program for the farmers and the agricultural community in western Canada, all the people whose future looks so bleak. In light of the information we have, what he has produced is entirely inadequate. The fact is that the agricultural industry in general and certainly in the west has fallen into disastrous conditions, a disastrous situation. This is something which is not temporary but shows all signs of becoming a permanent blight brought on to a large extent, we recognize, by world conditions but
Grain Payments
certainly aggravated by the fact that this government is, and for some years has been bankrupt of ideas and intelligence in this regard. In our view and in the view of the agricultural community there is a sense of sterility and defeatism, and this is apparent in the statement made by the minister today.
Just yesterday, Mr. Speaker, in a special report to the Economic Council of Canada by Mr. S. C. Hudson, former director of economics in the federal Department of Agriculture, made a statement that some of the main reasons for the difficulties, particularly in western Canada agriculture, are the lack of uniformity in the protein content of Canadian wheat shipments, a lack of flexibility in pricing and insufficient market development work. There are other criticisms but these alone I give to the House today because of the limited time at my disposal.
The growing feeling of frustration, anger and alienation in the west will not be eased but will in fact be compounded by the minister's statement. As practical people we in the west do not expect miracles and understand that problems of the nature of those which afflict us will require long-range treatment. Certainly not since 1963 have we expected or received too much from this government, but we did feel entitled at least to some understanding and to some sympathetic consideration and proof of determined effort to get at the root of the problems.
I suppose we should not have expected or hoped for too much understanding from a government headed by a Prime Minister who publicly indicates his indifference to the problems of selling wheat, but we did hope for something better from the western representatives on the government side, particularly those in the cabinet. Not only have they been ineffective in pleading the cause of the west but in my humble opinion they have ended up as collaborators in proposing completely unacceptable programs. I do not think that any other countries in the world are taking this defeatist attitude.
What about the problems of the manpower surplus which is being created? What about crash manpower programs? What about the regional incentive programs designed to meet situations of this kind? What about surpluses which may result from changing the emphasis from wheat to other crops? What about the surplus wheat which will result from this land which is being summerfallowed? These are all questions which need to be answered and have not been answered.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PAYMENTS FOR REDUCTION OF WHEAT ACREAGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement demonstrates the government's complete intellectual bankruptcy. After having bungled the whole question of Canadian wheat marketing, the best solution this government can offer is to pay the farmers for not producing wheat. This government has been in office for some seven years and has done nothing to adopt aggressive sales policies like those followed by our competitors in wiorld markets.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PAYMENTS FOR REDUCTION OF WHEAT ACREAGE
speechtext: And by the previous government.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PAYMENTS FOR REDUCTION OF WHEAT ACREAGE
speechtext:
It has continued using an anachronistic grading system. When some of our competitors were adopting a grading system based on protein content, this government continued employing a grading system which is out of date. Furthermore, this government allowed itself to be manoeuvred into dropping the old International Wheat Agreement and into organizing the International Grains Arrangement under GATT which eliminated the Soviet Union, one of our competitors, and left it free to do whatever it liked in this field.
The government also allowed itself to be manoeuvred into permitting an 11-month hiatus between the end of the International Wheat Agreement and the beginning of the International Grains Arrangement. The result was that during that period many of our competitors sold below the minimum price and continued selling below the minimum price even after the International Grains Arrangement came into effect. Canada was pushed more and more out of the market and some of our competitors have been successful in selling wheat, whereas we have not been as successful.
The best the government can do now is the program outlined today. When millions of people in a hungry world go to bed hungry every night, I submit it is the height of

insanity for a Liberal government to offer to pay farmers to take 22 million acres of land out of wheat production.
The minister's statement also represents a breach of faith with the wheat growers of western Canada. During the last election campaign the Prime Minister and some of his ministers said that the farmers could be sure that over a three-year period the government would be able to sell 1.3 billion bushels of wheat, an average of 433 million bushels yearly. On the basis of the price they were supposed to be guaranteed under the International Grains Arrangement, the farmers planted their wheat accordingly. The end result of all this is that the farmers have suffered a very drastic decline in their farm incomes in western Canada.
I notice that the National Farmers Union has sent the Prime Minister a bill for $385 million which it says is the difference between what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who was then Minister of Agriculture, said the farmers would receive and what they actually received. The loss of $385 million to the wheat producers of western Canada represents not only a disaster for them but a catastrophe for the whole western economy. And what is the government offering in exchange? It is not offering them a diversification program. Instead, by calculation and design it will prevent farmers switching over into the production of other crops or increasing their cattle and other livestock.
The government has now introduced an element of compulsion by basing the wheat deliveries in the crop year 1970-71 on how much land the farmer puts into either sum-merfallow or perennial forage crops. They are virtually preventing the farmers from going into diversification by insisting that if they want to sell the wheat they have on hand they should get out of production of coarse grains and Wheat to the extent of 22 million acres.
The government is offering the farmers in compensation $6 an acre for wheat land put into summerfallow and $10 an acre for land put into perennial forage crops. I remind the House that the only other time acreage payments were paid for crop reduction was during the war. In 1941, when wheat was selling at the local elevator at 50 cents a bushel, the farmers were paid $4 per acre. On that basis the government should be paying at least $8 or $10 an acre for land to be put
February 27, 1970	COMMONS
into summerfallow. A payment of $6 an acre will not begin to compensate the farmers.
The members of this House should not be under the impression that there is no cost involved when putting land into summerfallow or perennial forage crops. It costs money to buy forage seed and to put the land into forage crops. These amounts of $6 and $10 will barely, if at all, cover the cost of summerfallow and putting land into perennial forage crops. Where is the compensation for the loss of income arising from the fact the farmer is not able to grow and deliver wheat to the Wheat Board? There is no compensation for that at all. This is a very small sop to throw the farmers of western Canada who have been betrayed by this government on whose promises the farmers depended. They now find that those promises are completely worthless.
We cannot discuss this matter at length, Mr. Speaker, because we are on motions, but I submit to Your Honour and the government that an early opportunity should be provided during which this whole matter can be debated in the House. An opportunity should be given for the minister to be more specific about some of the details which we cannot get during the question period. I hope an opportunity will be provided next week so we can have a full debate on this question.
I am convinced that the wheat producers of western Canada and the people of the prairie provinces in particular will be disappointed and disgusted at this "Minnie" mouse that has been brought forth by the government after a long labour.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the House that after consultation with the Prices and Incomes Commission, I have informed the copper and copper concentrate producers, the secondary materials handlers and the copper fabricators, that as of March 1 the supply of copper into the domestic market will be assured at a level of 23,500 tons per month at a price of 59 cents per pound. Mr. David Orlikow (Winnipeg North)': Mr. Speaker, on January 1, 1969 the price of copper was 45 cents a pound. Before this last increase, about which there has been negotiation between the government and the copper producers, there had already been three increases concerning which the government made no comment. The result is that even taking into account the agreement on the part of the copper producers to limit their present price to 59 cents a pound, increases in the price of copper during the last 13 months amount to more than 30 per cent. This does not take into account the fact, which the minister has admitted, that the price of 59 cents a pound will not cover all the needs of Canadian users of copper; they will have to pay a good deal more for a substantial percentage of the copper they require.
This increase in price comes at a time when the profits of the copper producers-Noranda, Inco, Falconbridge, Texas Gulf-are higher than they ever were in the past. Their admitted profits, which are less than their actual profits, have been increasing by more than 10 per cent a year. The acquiescence on the part of the government makes it clear that price increases are not caused by wage increases. Price increases amounting to more than 30 per cent in one year amount to substantially more than any wage increases won by workers in the copper industry in that year. It is

also clear that the government's appeal to industry to hold any price increases which they may implement to a figure less than the actual increase in costs has been a failure.
There is no evidence that the copper producers demonstrated to the Prices and Incomes Commission or to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who made this statement today, that this increase to which the hon. gentleman is agreeing has been made necessary by increased costs or falling profits. It is obvious the increase is due to the fact that the world price of copper has substantially increased because of the shortage of copper. The copper companies are saying they are entitled to this increase because they could get more in the United States. I suggest to the minister and to the government that the workers in this industry or in any other industry would be less than human if they did not take the same attitude of being entitled to ask, fight for and get whatever the traffic will bear, just as the copper companies have done, and to ignore the pious appeals made by the Prime Minister and the hon. gentleman that they should show some restraint in the future.

speechtext:
that Bill S-19, to amend the Parole Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this somewhat brief bill is brought forward in order to rephrase two sections of the Parole Act to give them the meaning that they were thought to have when they were enacted by the Parliament of Canada and which they were thought to have by the administration having the responsibility for the act.
The first section sought to be amended in the bill is section 11A which was enacted last year in the Criminal Law Amendment Act providing that multiple sentences be treated

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
as a single sentence. The significance of that clause was to make clear the basis for computing remission. The object of section 11 A, when it was enacted, was to provide that multiple sentences of imprisonment be treated as a single combined sentence in calculating the term of imprisonment for the purposes of the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and the Parole Act. In habeas corpus proceedings in the courts last fall the section was interpreted in a way quite different from what it was thought to mean up to that point. The effect of the judgment, if I may summarize briefly, is that irrespective of the date that terms of imprisonment are imposed on an inmate who is in confinement serving a sentence, the date of the commencement of subsequent terms of imprisonment is the date on which he was originally confined.

speechtext:
This leads to absurdities and does not carry out the intention of Parliament or the court doing the sentencing. It was to remove the consequence of that decision that the clause was introduced here. I could give examples of the absurdities, but perhaps it would be better if I did that at the committee stage when the bill goes to the standing committee. It will be seen at once that the results flowing from that decision could be quite ridiculous and quite absurd.
The other clause of the bill seeks to amend Section 17 of the act. Section 17 of the Parole Act was amended by the Criminal Law Amendment Act of last year. The purpose of the amendment was to make clear in the statute that the term of imprisonment that a parole inmate must serve, whose parole has been forfeited by virtue of being convicted of an indictable offence, is a single term of imprisonment commencing on the date when the sentence for the indictable offence was imposed. It was also desirable to make it clear that the period of time for which the inmate was committed as the result of the forfeiture of parole included all the remission that had been granted to him. This amendment did not involve any change in policy but resolved any doubt that existed in respect of the practice that had been followed.
Section 13 of the Parole Act also has a retroactive aspect. The retroactive aspect of the amended section 13, when read together with section 17 of the act, results in inmates

not being credited with time spent in confinement in certain cases. This may occur when the forfeiture of parole follows a period during which the inmate has been confined under the Parole Act as a result of the suspension or revocation of his parole. It has also resulted, in rare cases, in inmates being credited with time towards the completion of their sentence during a period in which they were at large. These results were not intended and it is to correct these irregularities affecting a certain limited number of inmates that the amendment is sought for the purpose of clarifying the difficulties in that respect.
I think there is nothing more than I can usefully say at this stage in the debate because the amending bill does not raise any new matter of policy or principle. It merely seeks to clarify what was thought to be the law in the statute.

They are often criticized-I don't know whether by a quiet minority or majority-for being too soft with these people, but I am convinced that no one who has served time in a penitentiary ever

came out of that institution a better citizen. You might ask me what to do with him. I know what I would do. I would set up rehabilitation centres. If we can afford a new cultural program for the CBC to be initiated in 1972, surely we can afford to have that kind of justice for the greatest resource of all. Living is the basis of culture, a total man's experience. This is an experience. This is what culture is about.
I have reason to feel that they are just using this to keep me here as the people in Drumheller don't wish to have people there as I was told that this was just a letter and was irrelevant. Anyway I have written a follow up letter to him and asked for an answer one way or another about my appeal.
This boy is locked up in the penitentiary. There are no visitors and he has received no replies. He is entitled to one letter a month or once every two weeks. I am not sure of that regulation. I have not checked it. It used to be one letter a month. He is waiting.
If he answers me, then they will have to tell me the reason why when classified as medium security they are holding me in a maximum pen when there is really, I feel, nothing here I can do to help myself. I hope this is sufficient. Thank you.
This letter is signed by young Barr. His mother wrote me a letter, to which I replied on January 23, 1970 as follows:
I have written to your son asking him for details concerning his sentence and the charges laid against him.
As soon as I receive a reply I will have enquiries made to see if there is anything I can do to be of help.
The mother then contacted me by phone and I wrote to the boy as follows:
Your mother and father of 31 B. Normandy Crescent, Kingston, contacted me in reference to your conviction.
I would appreciate a detailed statement of the charges upon which you were convicted; statement of the facts, and whether there is any consideration to be given you in reference to the new system of parole whereby you would be permitted to work in the day time and return each night to custody.
It occurs to me that in Prince Albert this would not be possible but if you were moved to Drumheller then I think some negotiations in this regard would be more feasible.
When we talk about parole it sounds wonderful, but these things are happening. I do not know the percentages. We cannot bury our heads in the sand. Whether we like it or not, we are living in a day when in some educational institutions as high as 50 or 60 per cent of the students have used drugs. Think of the tremendous psychological trauma that occurs when a young boy is given three
February 27, 1970

years. He has been sitting in the same classroom with other students who have done the same thing and perhaps still are, yet he is incarcerated in the loneliness of a penitentiary.
I am a reformer. I started out to be one as a lawyer and I am still one. This boy is having his case presented in the highest court of the land today, Parliament. Every one of us feel this way. We do not agree on economic matters with the members of the New Democratic Party, but there is one thing for which I give them credit, particularly their leader. When he was Premier of Saskatchewan he had a sense of humanity. You could not help but have some affection for him, even though you differed in philosophy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night a somewhat unusual event took place in this chamber. The Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) received warm applause from all sides of the House. Usually a government spokesman receives warm applause only from the supporters of the government side. What took place last night indicates the affection and appreciation felt by hon. members for the efforts of the Solicitor General over the years in this Parliament. He has added greatly to the legislation. Some people say we might not have encountered the difficulties which prevailed with regard to rule 75C had the Solicitor General been dealing with this matter at the time. However, I shall not comment further on the point.
Parole Act
I should like the minister to add more diamonds to his crown. Before he retires I should like to see him bring forward legislation with regard to the annulment of criminal records. Yes, I know he has presented a bill which has been referred to committee, but the bill really does not go far enough. It is anaemic. I hope that by the time it comes out of the committee we shall have an effective measure.
I should like to see the minister bring forth legislation with regard to juvenile delinquency. When we note the wide disparity in jurisdiction across the country, I think we all agree it is time he did so. As a third effort, I should like to see the Solicitor General bring forth legislation to ensure a better and more effective parole system. Bill S-19 is really a housekeeping bill. The minister spoke only very briefly with regard to its contents and consequences. I would have liked the Solicitor General to bring forth a bill concerned entirely with the Parole Act. I thought he would have taken the initiative following the report of the Committee on Corrections which contained at least 50 pages on the inadequacy and shortcomings of the Parole Act and made specific recommendations which should be implemented so as to bring the legislation into line with modern requirements.
As the minister told us, the bill before us contains two main features. Concurrent and consecutive sentences are now to run from the dates on which the different sentences were imposed and not from the date upon which the first sentence was imposed. The second change makes clear which dates are to be taken into consideration when calculating the length of time a prisoner who has forfeited his parole must spend in prison, and the basis for calculating the amount of any remission to which he may be entitled. As the Solicitor General has stated, the first change follows a decision of the courts in which a judge ruled that time imposed for a subsequent offence committed by an accused should run from the date of the first conviction rather than from the date of the subsequent conviction. This change gives rise to certain problems. The provision relates to an offence which has been committed subsequent to a first conviction. The question which arises in my mind, and I hope the Solicitor General will think about it, is this: what happens with regard to an offence committed prior to the offence for which an accused has been sentenced?
The situation which arises very often in the courts, is this: a person is convicted of
4X80

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
one or two offences and is sentenced to a term in a penitentiary or in a reformatory. Then, before he gets to the reformatory or the penitentiary, other charges are preferred against him. He usually pleads guilty to the additional charges. A distinction must be made between offences in respect of which he has been charged, found guilty and sentenced, and offences committed prior to the offence on which he has been found guilty. The amendment before us relates only to offences for which an accused has been found guilty on charges which are laid subsequently. These are the main points, and I hope the minister will comment on them.
The second change concerns the length of time a person must serve when he has forfeited his parole. In 17(1) the amendment is set forth. It states:
When parole is forfeited by conviction for an indictable offence, the parole inmate shall undergo a term of imprisonment commencing when the sentence for the indictable offence is imposed, equal to the aggregate of-
And this is what I am concerned about
(a) the portion of the term to which he was sentenced that remained unexpired at the time his parole was granted, including any period of remission, including earned remission, then standing to his credit.
This indicates there are two types of remission. There is the statutory remission, which I understand amounts to one quarter of the sentence imposed, and then there is the earned remission which amounts to three days for every month of good behaviour. It is obvious from the amendment that the intention is to include in the term which a man must serve after the forfeiture of his parole not only the statutory remission but also the earned remission.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the one o'clock adjournment I was directing my remarks to the second change that the Solicitor General has requested in Bill S-19, namely that concerning the calculation of time once a person has had his parole forfeited. The burden of my remarks was that the Solicitor General has now included in the

calculation of this time the earned remission that the person was entitled to prior to release. I indicated that there are two types of remission: there is statutory remission, which is one quarter of the parolee's sentence; then there is earned remission, which is dependent upon good behaviour and amounts to three days per month.
According to the proposed new section, in calculating this time a person who has forfeited his parole will have the earned remission that is then standing to his credit added to the balance of his sentence, and it seemed to me that this was an unfair way of treating such person, even though he had forfeited his parole. It is much like a worker who works from Monday to Friday, and whose employer fires him on the Friday and tells him he is not entitled to wages from the Monday to the Friday.
That is analogous to what would happen here in the case of an inmate in a penitentiary who has earned remission for good behaviour. Because he has forfeited his parole and has been returned to prison, we are going to be vindictive and add to the balance of his term the remission days he earned while in prison. I understand his not being entitled to any earned remission while out on parole; but if the purpose of our parole system is to rehabilitate the prisoner, then under this change it seems to me he is being treated rather harshly, indeed to the point of our becoming vindictive.
Having set forth that objection to the second part of the bill, I should like to develop some ideas that touch on this problem of parole. At least 50 pages of the Ouimet comission report were devoted to the subject of parole. I should have liked the Solicitor General to introduce amendments to the Parole Act, amendments that are lacking in the present bill, to put Canada in the foreground in the treatment of parolees and in meeting the problems of parole.
At page 329 of the Ouimet commission report parole is defined in these words:
Parole Is a procedure whereby an inmate of a prison who is considered suitable may be released, at a time considered appropriate by a parole board, before the expiration of his sentence so he may serve the balance of his sentence at large in society but subject to stated conditions, under supervision, and subject to return to prison if he fails to comply with the conditions governing his release.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
On the following page the commission states that really parole is a treatment-oriented correctional measure, not a sentence-cor-
February 27, 1970

recting method. It is stated that parole is designed as a logical step in the total correctional process and is designed particularly to assist the offender's re-integration into the community as a contributing and law-abiding citizen. Again, they say that at the same time, for the offender, parole is an opportunity and a test of self-control and ability to get along in the community. These remarks really indicate what parole is all about.
Like the previous speaker, I must give credit to the chairman of the Parole Board and his associates for the tremendous job they have done concerning the problem of parole. In fact Mr. Street has made many speeches across the country in which he set forth what has been done in this field and the success that has been obtained. He pointed out that by keeping a person in prison the maintenance cost of such a person is roughly $5,500 a year and that when a person is placed on parole the cost of the parole amounts to $750.
There has been a great deal of success in respect of persons who have been placed on parole. They have obtained work in the communities at salaries and wages which add to the gross national product of our country. During the discussion of his estimates, the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) provided the members of the committee with certain details concerning the population of the penitentiaries. These details indicate that 74 per cent of all inmates range between age 20 and age 40; 7 per cent range between age 15 and 20 and the balance is made up of persons over 40 years of age. This indicates the necessity for excellent parole provisions concerning people in the group between 20 and 40 years of age because of the number in this group, namely 74 per cent. I also note from the figures that in the year 1967 there were four persons in penitentiaries who were 15 years of age and 15 persons who were 16 years of age. Surely, we have reached the point where we are not sending persons who are 15 and 16 years of age to penitentiaries. This is one of the most dreadful things that could happen with regard to the treatment of young offenders.
In a return tabled in the House, the Solicitor General pointed out the number of federal parolees, the number of violations and the number of persons returned to custody in the period 1960 to 1967. Through the years there has been an increase in the number of paroles granted. In the year 1967 1,328 federal paroles were granted. Of that number, 328 parolees
Parole Act
violated their parole conditions. There were 243 parolees returned to custody. The 1967 figures indicate that of the 1,328 paroles granted roughly 25 per cent of the parolees were in violation of their terms of parole and roughly 20 per cent were returned to custody. On the face of it, this would appear to be a rather high percentage. It would seem that we should direct our attention to the reason these parolees violated their parole.
The Ouimet commission report indicated some of the conditions that are imposed on a parolee. The report states that these conditions are not unreasonable. The commission did not recommend any substantial changes in this regard. I would imagine that the changes suggested by the minister are changes which probably have been recommended by the chairman of the Parole Board, and possibly the Commissioner of Penitentiaries as well as some other officials. It would seem to me that the persons who are missing are the parolees themselves. I should like to make a suggestion to the Solicitor General on which I hope he will act. When this bill is referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, I would suggest that the members of the committee visit some of the institutions in which federal inmates are confined and hear what some of these men have to say concerning the provisions, the effect and the operation of the Parole Act. I would recommend that the members of the committee visit Kingston Penitentiary, Dorchester, St. Vincent de Paul in Quebec and also a minimum security institution either at William Head or Springhill in order to obtain from the inmates information about the operation of the Parole Act. I am positive that to date the Solicitor General has not had representations from these people.
Two weeks ago I had the privilege of sitting with the Transport Committee in Toronto when it studied ways to improve the ground transportation at the airport and other places in Toronto because of the difficulties which obtained at the airport in respect of taxi service. At those meetings, the Committee on Transport heard many taxi drivers set forth their views concerning the problems at the airport. Many recommendations were made with regard to improvement. I must give the hon. member for LaSalle (Mr. Lessard), the chairman of that committee, full credit for his patience with and encouragement to the taxi drivers and others who set forth their views. If the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs were to make trips to certain institutions, and

I do not want to delay this bill very long. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) reminded us that parole is a treatment 
oriented concept. I think that he and others who have taken part in this debate have quite properly congratulated the board on the excellent program it has developed. I submit that the board would be the first to recognize that it tries to solve only part, admittedly the core part, of the total problem. I am thinking now of a young parolee who was recently released from Dorchester and is facing the really frightening prospect of getting himself a job and entering into the mainstream of life in the city of Toronto. There are many examples of this, and the officers of the board are exceptionally helpful.
But there are other aspects to this problem. Some of them are dealt with very effectively by the St. Leonard's Society, the halfway houses. Then, of course there are the Elizabeth Fry and John Howard Societies which obtain some funding from the government of Canada. I am thinking of the important links between the parolee and his integration into the community, and the frustration that he experiences in the community, despite the best Parole Act in the world, unless the concept is understood by a wide segment of the community. Otherwise, frustration and recidivism are bound to occur.
At Christmas time I had an opportunity to see something of the very close and effective work that the Canada manpower centres do in this field of service. I must admit that the manpower officer in the city of Saint John asked me to put his point of view to the minister, and this is a pretty good opportunity to do so. He feels that it is exceedingly important that the penitentiary service make available to manpower centres as much information as possible at the time when people can be expected to be released on parole.
In many parts of our country manpower officials have a pretty tough job, particularly where there is high unemployment. They have an added difficulty if the penitentiary service does not make available fact sheets. I forget the actual name of the form. We live in a world of forms and I cannot keep them all straight. But there is a sort of information sheet available on each person who is about to be paroled. So, I hope the minister and his officials will take this as a friendly and instructive criticism and suggestion that this information be made readily available to the manpower centres well in advance of intended parole. I think it happens in many cases now, but 1 am told by manpower officials that it is happening not as often as it should.
February 27, 1970

However, I understand that manpower officials quite properly visit the various institutions and, by way of interviews, receive some information on the people eligible for parole. I think this is a worthy objective.
I think that the chairman and members of the board are too modest about speaking about the achievements of the board since its inception. I know that a good many of the members of the board speak out on the subject, but I often wonder why they only preach to the converted. In other words, they often speak to professional people or people trained in the field, and I would make a plea for a stepped up series of statements or articles in the popular press about the board. I make no apology for this. I think that the story could be told in a rather dramatic form, not ladled on so to speak, but just told in some of the so-called popular magazines, both the church and the secular magazines of our country. Helpful as it is to have members of the board on the circuit, in my opinion nothing would be better than to have articles in the Weekend magazine, and other such magazines seen by a great number of Canadians, so that the public can understand that they have an extremely important role to play in the whole rehabilitation program.
We can have the most superbly drafted laws, but if there is no community acceptance of the concept, and the board and the minister are perfectly entitled to tell their story, then frustration will ensue. I hope to find in the months ahead a spate of articles on this subject, and I hope the minister will initiate them in the near future.
I want to make one other observation regarding the rather new phenomenon of the meetings of our judges. I know this is a delicate constitutional area, but I think that sometimes we are so delicate about the constitution that we resist some obvious initiatives. I think it has been very valuable that the judges, the sentencing officers of our system, have been having a good many more meetings on the problem of uniformity, in so far as there can be uniformity in a world as plural as ours. But this is an important departure and I hope it is followed up. I suspect- and I just voice this because the suspicion alarms me-that some magistrates who have not been gripped by the concept of parole, are imposing very substantial sentences, much more lengthy than they have before the parole system came in, and are turning over the problem to the board. I think this is not a good thing.
Parole Act
I noticed the other day, for instance, that in my own province a very young offender received 14 years for an infraction of the narcotics act. Obviously, there is an obligation, and an early one, on the parole board to rectify this sentence. But I would hope that judges, not only at the Supreme and Superior court level but on the magistrates level, across the country will step up the number of opportunities for getting together and discussing the whole matter of sentencing.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The drug problem is upon us whether we like it or not, and I suspect that long sentences, brutally long sentences, are going to have no appreciable effect on what is obviously the most serious social problem in the field of law that we have facing us today.
I congratulate the minister, and I am particularly happy to have an opportunity in public to say what many of us have found since coming to parliament, that the work of the parole board is worthy of our commendation and support.

I was pointing out that, although we have more than doubled the number of paroles, the number of persons that were returned to custody increased by less than 20 per cent. In other words, if we again doubled the number of paroles we granted, we would probably reduce that figure for those returned to prison to 10 per cent. The number apparently will be small, but this number will represent the hard core of recidivists who will always remain. If we increase the number of paroles, we do not necessarily increase the number of recidivists. So, I think the parole board has been overly cautious. I certainly could not congratulate them on the number of paroles they have granted because I don't think they have been excessive. There is one other point I would like to make. The prisoners themselves will give you a pretty good indication why parole is difficult, why they are dissatified with parole, and in many cases why parole does not produce the results we, the general public, want that parole to produce. A lot of the dissatisfaction comes from the fact that the inmates don't know the
parole board. They have never had an opportunity of meeting them. Then, as soon as the parole board considers all the factors involved, their recommendation is supposed to carry some weight with the people in the administrative field-

[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
One of the factors which the board takes into consideration, and it must, is the environment into which a prisoner will be

February 27, 1970

released. In many cases the type of environment you read about on paper is not necessarily the type of environment to which the prisoner will be returning. I am two years out of date, Mr. Speaker, because I have not discussed this matter at any great length with prisoners. However, I was very impressed with the charge made by prisoners, particularly in Kingston and St. Vincent de Paul, that the administrative officers with whom they deal are often not in a position to tell them why they failed to get parole or to give them any advice to help meet new criteria. Probably more important is the fact that neither the correction officers nor the inmates were too familiar with the decision taken by the board nor the grounds for it.
At that time I heard a number of prisoners state that they were not going to apply for parole; they just were not interested any more. I still think, Mr. Speaker, that if we had a good parole system in Canada we would have correction officers in the penitentiaries advanced enough in their role to know when a prisoner should be released.
I remember a prisoner who is in the news today, and we will probably hear more of him, whose mental attitude improved enormously when certain changes that affected him took place in the penitentiary. That was the time for parole, the time his correction officer should have recommended parole, should have insisted that the parole board take a look at the situation. The parole board was interested in giving him parole a year or so later but he was no longer interested. He felt discriminated against and persecuted and felt that he had to clear his name. In my opinion when he was released he was in a much worse mental state and not as able to take advantage of rehabilitation as he would have been at the earlier date. I discussed this case with the deputy warden, who was also of the opinion that the time had arrived for this person to be released. The parole board still thinks a little like the judges-he has not been punished enough, enough time has not gone by.
Surely, anyone who is interested in parole or correction should act on the proposition that when a person's mental condition will allow him to be absorbed into society without resentment or difficulty to that society, that is the time he should be released. As the member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said, judgments vary in the extreme. They vary on a regional basis and on a number of other factors. In my own area we used to
Parole Act
have a judge who suffered from ulcers and the sentences varied depending upon his medical condition on a particular day. The parole board, acting on behalf of Parliament and on behalf of society, should be able to make the decision on when a person can be accepted back into society.
If we only wanted to obtain free labour for the state, Mr. Speaker, we would put prisoners in the chain gang, as is done in Tennessee. We do not believe in that any more. Indeed, I do not think that Canada has ever been involved with that type of restitution, and I think most people would agree that we should not be involved in it. Today, many businessmen look at this figure of $5,000 or $6,000, which is the amount required to keep a prisoner in jail and decide, "My taxes are paying for it so I am going to do something about it. Send me some of these people and I will pay them, then I won't have to pay so much in taxes."
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, before we get carried away, that the parole board has not been that helpful or generous. They waited a long time, after those two accidents following their decisions of 1963-1964 to get back to where they were in the early 60s. I suggest there is still a considerable distance to go. I hope that the changes the minister contemplates in this bill will be put into effect. He says he has already started, but admits he is six months behind the report. My congratulations to him and to those people in the institutions who have made many changes.
I can remember going to the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary when the attitude of the guards and the prisoners was a disgrace. However, the last time I visited it, the atmosphere was totally different and improved. Great strides have been made in actual physical changes, but much more was being achieved through the change of attitude. A lot of this is due to our improved ability to train guards for these institutions.
We are plagued today, Mr. Speaker, with many problems in the penitentiary system and in the parole system that have no relationship to either of these bodies but stem from our lack of ability to keep abreast of social development in this country, as suggested by the hon. member for Broadview. Without changing the laws, we are making decisions about things that carry extreme penalties, such as the use of marijuana, which has become acceptable to a large segment of the population. In my opinion, no one in this House believes that a user of marijuana

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
should receive a five-year prison term as punishment. We are almost as tar behind as we were in the early days of prohibition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext: Or when they hanged people for stealing a sheep.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
That is right; or arresting a person for stealing food. It seems to me our society must change. I do not ask the parole board to make the decision for us, and I do not make the penitentiary staff responsible for the decision. I think we are closer to the judiciary than some of the other bodies and probably could have some influence on their decisions, which I think should better reflect public opinion.
On a number of occasions I have heard lawyers say, "If you have a bad law enforce it and somebody will change it." This may be so, and it may be the way to get changes, but it is very hard on some of our young people who feel the brunt of it. This must be a problem for the parole board and it is probably reflected in these figures, which are not broken down. We can put a young person in jail for five years for using marijuana, which is a non-habit forming drug. We can release him three days later and he is no more apt to take the drug then than six months later. No doubt there is a psychological problem as well as sociological problems involved, but there is no medical problem involved with this drug. Parole could take place two or three days after he goes to jail with almost as good a chance of success as five years later.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I am sure the parole board is not taking this fact into consideration and I really do not expect them to because of the hue and cry that would be heard from the judiciary. May I refer to something the Parole Board may not have considered. Would it not be a good idea to let out on parole all those people who are not dangerous and who would not benefit from being incarcerated but who would benefit if they were sent to university or some educational institution which could change their social attitudes? I think statistics will bear me out when I say that if you were to let almost all the prisoners out of penitentiary in this way you would not increase significantly the numbers who return to penitentiary a second, third or fourth time. It has been suggested that if you doubled the number you released on parole you would only increase by 10 per cent those who go back to prison a

second time. If you were to let out still more prisoners, very few of them, I submit, would become second or third offenders. This way of reforming our penitentiary system might be good. After all, the system we now have has not worked too well.
I have made these comments because, as the hon. member for Broadview said, the committee will learn much from talking to prisoners. On one occasion we interviewed 14 prisoners in St. Vincent de Paul who, in the opinion of prison authorities, were the most hardened criminals there, the prisoners who were serving the longest terms. When we questioned them we expected to hear them say that the newly appointed warden was not a good man. Yet in all cases, without exception, they did not make strong statements against the warden of the penitentiary but said instead that he had not been there long enough to change some of the bad conditions which had existed under the previous warden. They were all pleased the new warden had stopped the beatings which had taken place previously, that he had been influential in providing better food for the prisoners and had heeded what the correctional officers had said about prisoners in their reports to the warden.
Many prisoners like these will tell you they do not want parole. Many of them will not accept it. After all, it is no use paroling a prisoner who will pay no attention to the conditions of parole. Paroling such prisoners may not be of advantage to society. I suggest that if the committee were to talk to some of these prisoners it would be surprised at the forthrightness and honesty of the answers given. The opinions the prisoners have of themselves often coincide with the opinions of the John Howard Society, other rehabilitation agencies and the courts. I say this because it is clear that changes can be made in the system and because the minister, as I know, is interested in bringing in some real changes.
We all want to bring up to date our parole system and our penal system, while at the same time doing our best to provide for the hard core criminals who, for one reason or another, will always be with us. The least we can do is try to reduce their numbers to the very minimum by the use of parole. It is my opinion that the Parole board is doing a better job now than it has done for some time. I sincerely hope it will continue doing good work and take a few chances in paroling prisoners. The rewards will be great. It ought
February 27, 1970

to take chances in paroling prisoners, especially where the rewards are likely to be greater than average. Alter all, some of the board's members have been re-appointed over long periods of time and they should not be too scared to take chances in the interest of a better, more modern and more up to date penal system.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the paroling of prisoners is a very up-to-date and progressive move and for these reforms I wish to congratulate the department concerned. However, I do not want the minister or the department to think that this means the millenium has come in this field. So long as we have large numbers of people in our penal institutions and many failures in parole, much work remains to be done.
I wish to talk about a favourite subject, that of prevention. This is something the parole board thinks about a great deal. All those who interview young people who have run afoul of the law, and I am thinking of the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society and members of the parole board, are impressed not by how different these young people are but how shockingly normal they are. I will confine my remarks in the main to young people. I think the emphasis ought to be on prevention, because once they have been arrested it is almost too late. Mr. Speaker, 90 per cent of our crime comes from 10 per cent of our population. Most of the trouble results from the young peoples' insecurity in formative years.
The trouble arises because of broken homes and opportunities of fitting into our economic society, which is still a jungle, being missed. I think all those involved in parole and most law enforcement officers in Canada will tell you that most young people who run into serious trouble with the law have had little guidance. The guidance should begin of course with the mother in the home, and if it is not given there it should be given at school. Also, people involved in parole will tell you that many young law breakers are school dropouts. Therefore, these young people ought to be guided and encouraged at school. Teachers should not always be looking at the bright students in class and saying, "Here is a bright student; I have a potential Rhodes scholar in my class." They should be paying attention to the potential dropouts, to the so-called submerged 10 per cent of our students, and encouraging them to learn more. Perhaps, by staying after five o'clock at night or on Saturdays the teachers could keep in touch
Parole Act
with those students from less well-off homes to make sure they will not run afoul of the law.
By far the greatest number of offences in Canada today are offences against property. They are offences like petty stealing, the borrowing of the other boy's bicycle without his permission-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
Or robbing the bank.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
The end result is bank robbery, but that is not where it starts. By the time you get to the stage of bank robbery you have usually committed a long series of petty theft, break and enter, hanging around street corners, and are incapable of earning a so-called honest living. I agree with other hon. members who have suggested the Parole Board should embark upon an educational program for these young people before they get off on the wrong track.
A great responsibility is on the peace officer when he arrests a young person, because he is the first contact with the law. If he uses physical violence unnecessarily in the arrest because he is not getting the information required for a successful prosecution, he drives that young person, psychologically at least, into the arms of the criminal world. The young offender immediately feels buddy-buddy with all those who have been locked up under similar circumstances. Whether or not he is guilty of a serious crime such as stealing someone's property or committing an offence against society, he is from the start lined up on the wrong side of society. A peace officer must not use rough or brutal treatment because he may be the first friend the young fellow has had. He should be firmly treated, but not kicked and pushed down.
I like to think that the young people who appear in magistrate's court are not being herded off to jail but are being firmly and sensibly counselled. I like to think the forces of society are on their side, and they should know those forces are on their side. They should feel, by the way they are talked to and treated, that they are wrong and the court is right. I speak with some experience in this regard.
We should set up police colleges for our policemen. We cannot do very much with our young people until they come in contact with the law. We can do something with the police officers in whose custody these people are until they appear before the magistrate. The RCMP already has such a police college.

February 27. 1970
Parole Act
Every person who wears a badge of the law and who has the right to lay his hands on your child or any member of society should attend a police college and learn how to deal with these problems.
I suggest, also, that the magistrates should attend regular classes because most offences under our criminal law are dealt with by magistrates. Very often their training is not equal to the task. They would be the first to admit this. I do not suggest that only fully trained men in the legal profession should be magistrates-quite the contrary. But magistrates should know the rudiments of the law which they are enforcing. They should attend a college and receive training from knowledgeable men of their profession so they can dispense justice in a way that will help more young offenders to return to being productive members of society.
I am not going to say anything about the need for more judges and the bottleneck in the higher courts. Certainly in the magistrate's court today there is a great deal of delay. When young people are arrested they should be brought to court without delay. There is no need to detain a person two or three days without benefit of his family or the security of his home, when all he have done is be in the company of people who are suspected of doing something wrong. We need more scientifically trained policemen and magistrates.
Before the luncheon adjournment we were told about a young lad who was sentenced to a year in jail for every minute he was in court. I know from my own experience this often happens. It is wrong. There should be much more investigation into the background of young offenders. If we are going to take three years of a young man's life and keep him behind bars, we can afford to give him all the investigation necessary to find out how he got into that frame of mind, whether he had been trafficking in marijuana, stolen someone's bicycle or broken into a store. If this is not done, we are wasting the greatest natural resource we have in Canada-the future of our young people. Fifty years of productive life may go down the drain if we hastily dispose of the matter merely because a young person pleads guilty.
I suggest any person under 18 years of age who pleads guilty in Canada today is an idiot. If a young person does this without explaining his psychological, home and economic background, it should be proof enough-to put it in lawyers' language-that he is non

compos mentis. It might be a good idea if no one under the age of 21 was allowed to plead guilty. They should be presumed innocent until the Crown proves them guilty and they are put behind stone walls and iron bars for perhaps three of their most productive years.
A young person is put behind bars for only two reasons, to better him and protect society. When we put him in jail we should be sure that we have a program that will help him and society. I agree with those who say it does a man no good to spend three or five years in jail. I do not think people are completely sane who cold-bloodedly declare open war against society, say they are no longer going to work honestly, are going to rob banks, stick guns in the ribs of people, beat them over the head and snatch purses. However, if these people are under 21 years of age we should be very leary about entertaining a plea of guilty and accepting the responsibility of taking away three years of their liberty unless we know what they are, who they are, and why they did it.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
If our excuse is that we cannot afford to set up the proper courts to listen, or that we do not have the time, we cannot say we are in any better position than they are; we are showing that we are so mean and self-centred in connection with providing the proper type of courts that we can no longer pretend to be meting out justice. Parole then becomes a farce, because it is no use putting a boy on parole after he has been in jail for three years, under present circumstances, particularly if he should not have been there in the first place.
It would call for a great effort on the part of the John Howard Society, or the Elizabeth Fry Society if the prisoner happened to be a woman, to explain that society was right all the time. We should deal with our young people with a sense of understanding, taking advantage of the knowledge available through modern psychology, looking carefully at the medical evidence and the economic opportunity available-the chance to get a job in the situation in which the person accused of committing an offence found himself.
What often happens is that a boy will say he was educated only up to grade three and left school in trying circumstances because his home was broken up. Since then he had been trying to earn his own living in some ghetto. Then we ask him: Why do you not have the money to hire a good lawyer and
February 27, 1970

pay for the expensive red tape which the bureaucrats demand? He cannot have his case reheard because it costs 25 cents a word to have the evidence typed out. He does not have 25 cents; if he had, he would not have been involved in petty theft, petty marijuana trafficking or an offence of that kind which looks very bad until you know the background.
He might have been smoking marijuana because he could not stand the strain. I do not say he should be allowed to smoke marijuana, but if society is to become believable in the eyes of these young people we must be as pure as Caesar's wife; we must show them that it is not for lack of willingness on our part to put up the money that we are locking them in jail without a proper hearing or rehearing.
I know whereof I speak, because as a peace officer I had to deal with such people. I listened to them, I talked to them through the bars, and sometimes I did not know what to do because there were no financial resources available to give them the kind of help which would at least have left them satisfied in their minds. I was careful to treat them as human beings while they were in my charge, by seeing they were properly fed and spoken to and not bullied, cajoled or threatened into making confessions in one form or another. They have written to me from jail saying they did not know there was no such thing as British justice until they landed in jail. That is a sad commentary on our much vaunted legal and fair society.
This is the problem we face. I am afraid the Parole Board is often working against heavy odds when after four or five years of injustice it tries to do something the need for which might well have been avoided in the first place. Then again, the harm was doubly exaggerated by the kind of treatment these boys received after they fell into the toils of the law.
If hon. members do not believe this is true, I challenge them to visit our places of confinement. In most cases the warden would be very pleased to have them go there. When these boys are interviewed, over and over again they tell the same story. They are not at all convinced that they were wrong. Again, I am not soft: I would not be soft after 23 years of the kind of life I have led. But I know there is much truth in what they have to say and I know that if these roadblocks are removed there is a possibility that it will be seen they have not had a fair deal.
Parole Act
In many cases it will be found that somewhere along the line a little humanity, a little help, a little readiness to listen may change their whole attitude. Even hardened criminals have turned from a lifetime of crime and become productive members of society because they found some person, possibly a guard or a warden, who treated them like a human being, or even because in the last days of their confinement they met a representative of the John Howard Society or a member of the Parole Board who was ready to help them on the road back. This is why I congratulate the Parole Board and those who are working so hard at the retrieving end. It is also why I ask hon. members to bear with me for a few minutes while I ask whether there is not more we can do on the preventive side.
Twenty years ago the Mounted Police had a forward-looking program called the Youth and Police Program. I believe it was cancelled in the name of economy. This is not the first time I have stood in this House and said that when this program was undertaken by wellmeaning members of the Mounted Police, juvenile delinquency, which was at the root of the matter, dropped dramatically. When the young people of any community learn to-yes, I will use the word-love the policeman, there is no problem of juvenile delinquency on anything like the scale to which we are accustomed. When they see a police car, no tongues go out, there are no hisses or catcalls.
The cost of these programs to the Canadian public was negligible; however, the results not only in terms of broken glass saved but broken lives and broken careers mended was beyond calculation. The story of what happened in one small town in New Brunswick is well known and it is on record. Events there bear me out. The authorities closed the regular sittings of the juvenile court because one young man set up a boxing class. How much did it cost to get a few boxing-gloves donated by well-disposed citizens? How much did it cost to set up a few ropes in the curling rink when it was not in use and get these young men trying to punch each other on the nose under the Marquis of Queensbury rules, instead of meeting in some back alley, smoking marijuana and practicing mayhem?
There will always be hard-core prisoners. Some of the prisoners in the penitentiaries speak of the old alma mater. They wear the old school tie. They have their homo clubs going. They think they are running the penitentiary according to their own ideas. These

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
are no places to send any unhardened criminals, not even for 24 hours. We need new physical plant. I realize it is difficult for the minister to obtain the appropriations necessary for this purpose. I am sure he raises this matter and argues with his colleagues about it. But we must have additional plant; there must be an opportunity to segregate prisoners.
I know the minister and those responsible for law enforcement understand this well and are doing everything they can. We need more personnel of the right kind. We need more prison psychologists and doctors who can help in this regard. We also need a great deal more understanding on the part of the public. We have to reach the point at which we do not think that because a young man is put in jail he should no longer be allowed to visit his girl friend or receive more than one letter in two weeks, or whatever the period may be. I think he should be allowed to write all the right kind of letters he can. He must keep in contact with the decent side of society.
We should no longer punish married people by imposing long sentences of imprisonment in circumstances in which the woman is expected to live alone, apart from her husband, for a period which may be as long as ten years. What are we doing to her, perhaps an innocent victim of a terrible situation? Do any within the sound of my voice, or do any who may read what I have to say, think for one minute that in circumstances like that, after seven or eight years a person could be readily rehabilitated into normal society?
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Even if you are able to control yourself with prayer and meditation, what kind of strain is put on the family never to see the father or the mother, or to have family communication of any kind? I say a long period is not required. These offences occur when the family is already shaken, and nothing is accomplished by this sort of inhuman segregation of members of families by imposing long terms of imprisonment. If the real aim of prison is to return a man to a productive society, not only for personal reasons but on the ground of making him a civilized human being once more, I suggest we should do away with the sort of sadistic cruelty that is a hangover of the dark days of the Middle Ages.
The same is true of our young people. Take the case of a young man who has committed what may be a minor crime, at least in the

criminal sense. We are going to deprive him of social contact with the young lady of his choice. No longer will he be able to talk to her, hold her hand or pass the time of day, at least not more than once a month. This isolation does him irreparable harm. The fact that a young man of normal courage and instinct is deprived of his liberty should be shock enough; certainly it lets him know we no longer approve of the conduct for which he has been incarcerated.
With regard to sentencing and its effect on parole, I see nothing wrong with long and severe sentences for persons such as pushers of dope. But even there it might well be that a sentence hanging over a man's head will do more good than locking him up in a tank. If he is told to be of good behaviour or go to prison for ten years, this might well be the case, though I would leave it to the psychologists and prison experts to decide what will be a reasonable time after which to allow him out on parole and see whether or not he will again defy society.
We should also recognize that people in jail should not be regarded as slaves. Where possible, a prisoner should be allowed to earn money by the sweat of his own brow. We have taken away his liberty: in return he should be allowed to earn money which would be put in a trust fund until he is paroled. When he is paroled we should not necessarily give him the $2,000 or $3,000 that he had accumulated if he had been in prison for a long time, but we should give him a certain amount with which to rehabilitate himself. This could be regarded as rehabilitation pay and he would commence to earn it as soon as he went to jail.
When a prisoner leaves jail he enters a very difficult period of adjustment. For him it is like coming into the sunshine having been too long in the dark: he is blind for a while, lost in society. Any parole officer who knows his job will tell you that the first six months after being released from jail, at a time when a prisoner is trying to find his feet and is very proud and touchy, is a very difficult period. This is because the prisoner finds employment hard to come by.
If he does gain employment, he thinks that the next man on the lathe is watching him all the time, in the same way that for the previous three or four years, or whatever it was, he was kept under surveillance 24 horurs a day. He feels self-conscious. He has lost his pride. Worst of all, perhaps, he has no money, no means of economic support. Perhaps he
February 27, 1970

went to jail for stealing a car because he did not have the money to buy one. When he is released from prison again he has no money to buy a car and he feels crippled financially. He does not feel responsible to himself. His spirit has been bent, if not broken. He is convinced that society has no use for him, and he is self-condemned.
If the prisoner had been taught a trade in the penitentiary, making tin cans, army boots or sewing overalls, he would have earned an honest dollar, money that he knows will be coming to him. It would not be charity. Many people on parole do not want the John Howard Society to hold their hand; similarly, a young woman does not want the Elizabeth Fry Society to tell her how to behave decently. In some cases the prisoners think their lives are not much worse than the lives of those who put them in jail.
If they were able to earn by the sweat of their own brow money which had been put into a trust account for them, they would be put on the street in a way we would like to be treated. You cannot rehabilitate people in halfway houses as fast as you can when you give them money which they have earned. This gives them responsibility and presents them with a challenge to go back into the world and become the normal people they were before they entered prison.
We must remember that these people have had a fall from grace. They committed a crime and were caught. They were given a fair trial-at least, I hope they were, though unfortunately in a good many cases they were not. However, we are putting a tremendous onus upon them to regain their place in society, and we should give them the economic means of so doing. This is more difficult for those who have nothing but the labour of their own hands to turn to. Those who are highly educated and have a Ph.D. can probably step into lucrative employment straight away these days, with our broadminded approach to rehabilitation. Not so the labourer. If he cannot put his $1 on the counter to buy beer along with his pals, he is a second-class citizen.
