speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member of this House who has just spoken made a most interesting presentation based on his knowledge as a member of the House of Commons, his interest in penology and, most of all, on what he learned and understood as, shall I say, a humanitarian when he was a member of the Royal Canadi-
Parole Act
an Mounted Police. I think hon. members should pay particular attention to what he said.
If my memory is correct, for many years he was called upon to arrest and to jail those who had broken the peace. In the hon. member's case, his interest did not stop with arresting and jailing; his interest was-and still is-what happened to those prisoners afterwards. That is why I wish to emphasize the importance of what the hon. member has been saying these past few minutes.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
My position is a little different. I have had an interest in penology in all its aspects for the past 35 years. I have had this interest as a member of the provincial legislature of British Columbia and for almost the past 17 years in this House of Commons. This is not a passing interest; it is an interest that took me to see a man hanged in order that I could understand one aspect of capital punishment. In pursuing this interest I have made until now at least five visits to our penitentiaries every year.
I do not believe in guesswork, and therefore I visit the penitentiaries. During my visit to a penitentiary I have met from five to, on one occasion, 138 inmates in three days. So, Mr. Speaker, I believe I can safely say I have a keen and true interest in penology and I understand that if one breaks the law he must pay the penalty. But I also believe that our Canadian system of penology should not be based on revenge but on rehabilitation.
I sincerely regret that I must say Canada has not yet learned the meaning of modern penology and rehabilitation. We are so confoundedly stupid in respect of governmental decision and in respect of the building of our penitentiaries that in recent years we built a maximum security penitentiary which included aspects that were wiped out in the United States 60 years ago because they were considered to be inhuman. This is what we do in respect of penitentiary construction. If we are 60 years behind in construction, it is perhaps understandable and regrettable that we are so far behind in respect of parole.
Bill S-19 is a bill to amend the Parole Act. What is it? It is a bill containing two items of housekeeping; that is all it is. In this session we have a bill to amend the Parole Act which does not contain a damn thing concerning modern penology or modern parole systems, and which does not show that the government

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
has any understanding ol the procedure concerning rehabilitation or any belief that this should involve anything better than recidivism, the return of people who break the law to our jails and penitentiaries.
Mr. Speaker, I know I am not alone in saying we expected more in this session of Parliament than a couple of housekeeping measures in a bill to amend the Parole Act. We expected that Canada would start to catch up with the meaning of rehabilitation, and would initiate new policies to prove to those who break the law and have to pay the penalty that we are prepared to forgive them by giving them an opportunity to leave the penitentiary on parole under a parole system which does not involve outmoded regulations and procedures which a human being has to break. Do you want to know what I mean by that, Mr. Speaker? Some people will not like this, but I will tell you. Every man has the same considerations whether in penitentiary or out. If a man has been in a penitentiary for two years, five years, ten years or more and suddenly finds himself out in society he is going to blow his top.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext: That is right!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext: There are two things he might do. He might get drunk, or he might buy a woman. Right?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext: Of course.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSECUTIVE AND CONCURRENT SENTENCES, EFFECT OF FORFEITURE
speechtext:
Of course. So he breaks his parole, and immediately he has lost his whole period of parole. If he celebrates with beer and a woman, he breaks his parole and is back for the entire term of his original sentence. I do not know; I suppose the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) is as old as I am, but there are a good many people in jail who are not. Why do we not face the facts of life? Why do we not understand that men who have been inside prison walls in cells should be given a chance to explode a little? But no, not under our parole system!
There certainly is nothing in this bill that indicates a recognition of human nature. No matter how many years a person spends in penitentiary, he has only a few dollars when he comes out-and then what happens? He tries to get a job. Mr. Speaker, I say through you to the members of the House of Commons that I have known, not one but dozens of persons who have come out of penitentiaries in Canada, have obtained a job and learned the next day that someone has

phoned the employer and said, "Do you know that the man you just hired is out of penitentiary and is guilty of a criminal offence?"
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In one case a man was fired from six successive jobs because a policeman phoned the employers and asked, "Do you know who you have employed?" I think the Parole Act should provide that once a man has served his sentence he should not be prejudiced by our law enforcement officers when he is trying to get a job and holding it. I will go further than that. A man who is incarcerated for over two years in the penitentiary earns so much money. When you take off the few cents a day he is allowed for his canteen costs, he may end up with $50 to $100 on his discharge. He has to become rehabilitated and find a job.
I have suggested for years in this House that since by law a man must work in the penitentiary, we would be saving money as taxpayers if we paid unemployment insurance, so that when a man comes out of the penitentiary on parole and blows the little money he has-and, for God's sake, who blames him for blowing it-he has the basic security of unemployment insurance for three or six months until he can get himself established. This is part of parole.
Has the Solicitor General gone into these matters? Is he interested in them? Not according to the bill in front of us, the only Parole Act bill we have considered this session. It costs approximately $5 a day for every man and woman in the penitentiary. Other countries recognize this fact and act accordingly, as they do in the federal penitentiary system of the United States. If you break the law, you serve a sentence. But if you want to, and do, co-operate then as an inmate why should you not go out and work in industry and come back to jail at night or at the weekend? You get union wages for your work. The inmates are charged for their room and board, and they maintain their families.
We are making a slight start in this direction in Canada, but there is nothing in this bill that would make it a definitive policy. There is nothing in this amending bill to show that we understand parole is granted not only when a man has served a quarter, a third or half of his sentence, but that it could start from the day he began to serve his sentence with understanding for and acceptance of his responsibility.

I would be the first to say that if we had a progressive attitude to parole, a modern understanding of penology, and followed it through, and the parolee broke his parole, we should put him back in the cell behind bars, because if he will not accept responsibility that is where he belongs. But I firmly believe, from visiting our jails and penitentiaries over 35 years and listening to thousands of people in them, that if we could convince them we are interested in their rehabilitation, and not in revenge, and gave them the opportunity for rehabilitation by saying they were under our control but outside the cell and the prison walls, there would be far less recidivism than there is today. We would reclaim many more of them to a social rather than an anti-social attitude, and would thereby save millions of taxpayers dollars which are now being wasted because of our outdated understanding of penology and our outdated approach to the probation and parole systems.
I hope you agree, Mr. Speaker, that I have been speaking on the principle of this bill all the way through my remarks. I am heartbroken and disgusted that in the first session of a new Parliament, all that the government has introduced to amend the Parole Act is a couple of housekeeping measures. I speak most sincerely on this matter, as did the hon. member who preceded me and who can perhaps speak with more authority than I can, having been a sergeant in the RCMP for many years.
We hope the government, in the interest of rehabilitating those who have broken the law, in the interest of humanity and in the interest of the taxpayers, will take a new look at our system of penology and will try to learn from the experience of countries outside Canada, even some that are supposed to be heathenish. I have heard some people say how wrong it is, oh my God, to allow conjugal relations inside prison, as is the case in some countries. What is wrong with that? The biological urge of a man in prison is no different from that of a man outside.
I hope the Solicitor General and the government will take a new look at our system of penology and before this session is over will bring in a few comprehensive and understandable amendments to the Parole Act. Let us lead the world in this regard, not follow it.

The debate has been wide-ranging and I suppose one might say it went far beyond the bill that is before the House for consideration. But if it did, I have no complaint because while it was far-ranging it covered problems of major concern to society today, and I for one was glad to hear the expressions of opinion of the hon. members who took part. In the few minutes at my disposal before we adjourn I shall try to deal with some of the points raised by hon. members. I will leave other points to be dealt with at the committee stage of the bill.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) spoke at length about sentencing which, while it is of real concern, of course, is not directly related to this bill or the Parole Act. It is a subject which comes under the responsibility of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and has to be dealt with in another context in legislation dealing with sentencing.
The parole process should not be thought of as a review of sentence but rather as a part of the corrections program for persons who have been convicted and sentenced. It is important that it not be regarded as a process of appeal against sentence. I believe that would be fatal to the whole concept of corrections work and would destroy the program that is under way. Rather, it must be used aggressively in the corrections program so that once a person is convicted he is rehabilitated in the quickest and most effective way possible, and assisted to that end.
The hon. member also referred to a particular court case. He was good enough to give me the name of the case after the noon recess. Of course, the authorities will be looking into that matter at once. It would perhaps be inappropriate for me to comment on the case because I do not have detailed information about it. In any event, it is better done by the Parole Board authorities, who have all the files and information before them, rather than my speaking to it without having the necessary information.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) made an interesting speech and I shall make some comments on it. He spoke about the bill being a housekeeping bill dealing with the Parole Act. Of course, that is precisely what it is, what it was intended to be and what it is put forward as being: it is not intended to be anything other than that. I did not quite understand his desire to have the

February 27, 1970
Parole Act
Parole Act amended, because the Parole Act was amended extensively in 1969 and would seem to give authority for any or all of the propositions that have been asserted today. The problem does not lie in inadequate legislation governing parole; it is one of pressing forward with reform in this area, taking advantage of all the knowledge we can acquire on the subject and using it intelligently.
The rate of reform in this area is very rapid. With respect to the parole figures that were used in the debate, I am afraid there was a misconception. The hon. member was using the figure of paroles granted two or three years ago in respect of federal institutions only, but as the number of persons who returned to prison because of breach of parole he was using the figure applicable to all paroles granted whether the person was in a federal or provincial institution. That led to some confusion and I sought to correct it by asking a question later in the proceedings. The number of paroles granted in 1969-the figures are available right up to the end of last year-was 4,796. That was an increase from 1,750 granted in 1964. Therefore, it will be seen there is a very rapid increase in paroles granted.
The use of day parole has sharply increased. The number of day paroles granted or used, mainly for students returning to school during the day or to university, as the case may be, was 487 last year. Day parole is also used in other circumstances that perhaps can be elaborated on in committee. But it is interesting to note that the use of day parole has sharply increased over the years and how satisfactory it appears to be in the case of young offenders either still at school or who were students before they ran afoul of the law. It is used in order to keep them in their training processes at school or university.
Some rather complimentary remarks were made about the Parole Board, which I was very glad to hear and with which I heartily agree. I appreciate its work very much. I think it is a board that is working efficiently, and I want to make it very clear that we wish to continue that process in the future. It must be a continuing process. This is no place to sit back and rest on the laurels already won. There is an advance to be made in the years ahead. I believe we have one of the best corrections systems in the world today, that we have done a great deal very rapidly but that we have a great deal more to do, which is what interests me and must receive atten-

tion. Reference was made to the Committee on Corrections' report. At the moment that report is receiving very active study by the government. For example, 14 of the committee's recommendations relating to parole are already in operation and the work is going forward very rapidly.
Other hon. members made interesting suggestions, Mr. Speaker. I would like to take the time to comment on them all, but I think it is the sense of the House that I should not do so at this moment. I heartily concur. This is one area in which I feel we have not been as successful as we should have been. I welcome the opportunity of appearing before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs with the estimates of the department, when the whole subject can be pursued in detail. I should add that at the start of this session I suggested to the committee that they visit the penal institutions of this country. I have made that suggestion several times since the opening of the session, the last occasion being as recently as Wednesday of this week. I would hope we could arrange to do that as soon as hon. members are ready.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

I would hope that when we visit that institution it is to participate in the start of the physical destruction of a major part of it. I believe the hon. members concerned would share with me the pleasure of starting the physical obliteration and destruction of some of the old wings of the St. Vincent de Paul institution.

speechtext:
that Bill C-31, to amend the Canada Evidence Act (incriminating statements), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, one of the things we Canadians cling to is the idea that the administration of justice in Canada is not only fair but is felt to be superior to the administration of justice in the United States. In recent years, however, decisions by the United States Supreme Court have been responsible for a number of protections being afforded to anyone under arrest, and for restrictions on the police. These protections are unknown in Canada.
My bill has been drafted to put into effect the recommendations made by the United States Supreme Court. I take no credit for the drafting, Mr. Speaker; it was done at my request by a former associate of my colleague the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), Mr. Theodore Matlow who has had years of experience in the field of criminal law. I am satisfied that the draft which he prepared follows very closely the proposals made by the United States Supreme Court.
I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from the New York Times dated June 14, 1966, in which are summarized the views of the United States Supreme Court both in the news article and in the substantial excerpt from the decision:
The Supreme Court announced today sweeping limitations on the power of the police to question suspects in their custody-
The suspect, the court said, must have been clearly warned that he may remain silent, that anything he says may be held against him and that he has a right to have a lawyer present during interrogation.

February 27, 1970
Canada Evidence Act
If the suspect desires a lawyer but cannot afford one, he cannot be questioned unless a court-appointed lawyer is present.
If the suspect confesses after receiving the required warnings but without having counsel, the burden is on the prosecution to prove a knowing waiver of rights. And any prolonged interrogation will be taken to show a lack of waiver.
Mr. Speaker, I want to quote just one paragraph from the decision. Chief Justice Warren said:
When the defendant denied the accusation and said, "I didn't shoot Manuel, you did it," they handcuffed him and took him to an interrogation room. There, while handcuffed and standing, he was questioned for four hours until he confessed.
During this interrogation, the police denied his request to speak to his attorney, and they prevented his retained attorney, who had come to the police station, from consulting with him.
There are many cases, although not quite as bad, of a similar nature in Canada. I shall refer to one example before spelling out what my bill would do. I refer hon. members to the Steven Truscott case, but it is not my intention to discuss today whether Steven Truscott was guilty of the crime for which he was tried and convicted. I point out, however, that Steven Truscott was picked up by the police; he was 13 or 14 years old; he was taken to the police station; he was questioned for longer than three or four hours. During the time he was being questioned his parents came to the police station but were not allowed access to the boy. At no time were the boy or his parents made aware of the fact that he had the right to have counsel present when being questioned. It is true that Steven Truscott did not confess, but I submit that the whole course of the trial would have been substantially different had counsel been present while he was being questioned. That right was not given to Steven Truscott. My bill would, if enacted, provide the following:
3.	No statement shall be admisisble in evidence against its author in any criminal trial or other criminal proceedings against him unless it is first proved to the satisfaction of the court that it was made voluntarily and without any threat of harm or promise of gain by a person in authority.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
4.	No statement shall be admissible in evidence against its author in any criminal trial or other criminal proceedings against him if such statement was made while its author:
(i)	was in the custody of any person in authority or;
(ii)	reasonably believed that he was in the custody of a person in authority,
unless it is first proved to the satisfaction of the court that immediately prior to making such statement, its author was duly warned by a person in authority that:

(i)	he was not required to make any statement;
(ii)	if he voluntarily chose to make a statement, it would be taken down in writing and might later be used in evidence against him;
(iii)	he was legally entitled to legal counsel and that if he could not afford counsel, one would be assigned to act on his behalf if he so desired.
5.	(a) If, pursuant to section 4, a request for counsel is made, it shall forthwith be made known to a justice having jurisdiction who shall make all investigations that he shall require to inquire into the financial means of the person on behalf of whom the request for counsel was comunicated;
(b) If the justice believes that the person who requested counsel has not sufficient means to obtain counsel, he shall forthwith assign counsel to act on behalf of that person.
6.	(a) No person shall be interrogated by any person in authority after such person has requested counsel until such person has had a reasonable opportunity to confer with his counsel;
(b) Every person is entitled to the presence of counsel during all interrogations by a person in authority.
7.	No statement shall be admissible in evidence against its author in any criminal trial or other criminal proceedings against him if he was without the benefit of counsel at the time the statement was made unless it is first proved to the satisfaction of the court that the author knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to counsel provided by this act.
One need only visit the magistrate's courts or read any Canadian metropolitan newspaper for a couple of months to realize that people are frequently denied the right to counsel. There was a case in Toronto in the summer of 1969, a few months ago, involving Mrs. Shirley Hunter. She suffers from a sickness that makes her appear drunk, and she was involved in a slight accident and taken to the police station. When she tried to telephone her husband, the telephone was torn out of her hand. Her husband was called later and notified she was in jail but he was not permitted to see her. She was kept in jail overnight. The damage to her emotional and nervous system was considerable. As I say, she was not allowed to call her husband, she was refused bail and was not permitted to see counsel after her arrest.
In 1966 there was a case involving an Ottawa girl, Ann Lalonde, who had gone to Toronto. Ostensibly, her offence was being a vagrant in Yorkville. Here I am not concerned with whether she was guilty or not; I am concerned more with the magistrate's attitude. She appeared before Magistrate Donald Graham. Naturally, a young 17-year old girl from Ottawa who visits Toronto will not have a lawyer. I wish to read part of the discussion between Magistrate Graham and the girl, if
February 27, 1970

what took place can be termed a discussion. The magistrate said:
You wander, all day. You've got to tell me where you're going to stay in the next week or so, or you're going to stay in custody. Why can't you go back to Ottawa?
The girl replied:
Because I don't want to.. .1 had my own room the other week. There is nothing wrong with that. It is not against the law.
The magistrate said:
It is against the law, that is why you are here. Where are you living now, today, where is your room?
Later the magistrate said:
Well, we don't need you in Toronto and we don't want you wandering around. You'll get a decent place to live and you'll get a decent job if you're going to stay here, or you'll stay in custody-
And so on and so forth. The magistrate was giving his opinion when he said a person ought to have a decent job-a decent job being one that he no doubt approved of. I may agree with the magistrate. The point is that throughout the trial the magistrate consistently behaved in a way he would not have behaved had counsel been there to represent the girl. The magistrate did that only because the girl appeared in court without a lawyer. He would never have spoken to her that way if she had been represented by counsel, because he would have known that counsel would have taken the case to appeal and the appeal court very firmly and in no uncertain terms would have commented on what happened during the trial below.
I say this because I assume magistrates who are appointed have some knowledge of the law. I see the hon. member from Ottawa shaking his head. That really disturbs me! Every person in the land-not just businessmen, Members of Parliament, professional men and professional criminals, who certainly know their rights-should have the chance to be represented by a lawyer. They should not be required to make a statement to the police or to be questioned until the lawyer, if they want one, is present.
I repeat that every person ought to enjoy a fundamental right in Canada, the right to be represented by counsel at preliminary proceedings in order to make sure he is later given a fair trial. That is the position the United States Supreme Court has taken. It has spelled out the rights of the people and said that if the police, prosecuting attorneys or authorities ignore those rights, any convictions based on proceedings which have contravened those rights may be set aside.

I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) may propose legislation along those lines in future, together with other changes to the Criminal Code, in order to spell out the rights to which ordinary people are entitled. I hope hon. members will support the principle of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I admire what the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has in mind, I cannot go as far as he would, nor would I like to see the principle of the recent United States decision codified into our law. Bill C-31 would add part IV to the Canada Evidence Act to exclude statements made by an accused or suspected person during the investigation of an alleged breach of the Criminal Law unless taken under circumstances which provide the maximum of protection to him.
Generally speaking, under this bill the statement would be excluded unless the author was warned (1) that he was not obliged to make a statement; (2) if he did, it would be taken down and used against him; and (3) that he was entitled to have a lawyer present and, by inference, that that lawyer would be paid for by the province or the federal authority. All the lawyer would have to do if he must be there is say to the accused person, "You need not give a statement" and for all practical purposes all statements would be wiped out.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Certainly, sometimes there is abuse in taking statements; there is no question about that. But against this, do we take such a drastic step as to do away with, for all practical purposes, the use of the statement or confession and thus assist the criminal element, or at least a branch of society in which many turn out to be convicted criminals? The law up to now, as I understand it, is that in Canada, as in other common law nations, the confession must be voluntary. If there is any flattery of hope, or torture of fear present in the statement, it is excluded. The rules are not rigid. They are flexible. As has been the custom for centuries under British common law, there is discretion on the part of the trial judge. He makes the decision and usually after a trial within a trial he satisfies himself that the statement was voluntary.
Under the law as it is today, a lawyer need not be present when the accused is being questioned. If a lawyer is called, he will usually say to his client, "Don't talk until I get

February 27, 1970
Canada Evidence Act
there." I believe most lawyers take the further precaution of phoning the detective and saying, "I talked to my man and told him not to talk. If he does talk, I am going to be most suspicious." In my experience, that usually works. I think our flexible rules, which are growing and giving more protection, are quite good.
I think the first two points mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) could be codified, namely; that an accused must be warned that he need not give a statement and that if he does it will be taken down and may be used against him. With regard to his suggestion that a lawyer should be present and paid for attending on behalf of the accused, it is not possible as the law is today. The only way a lawyer could be paid by a province is if legal aid has been introduced, as it has in Ontario; but it has not been introduced in many of the other provinces.
But I wish to deal with the suggestion at a higher level. Do we want to go as far as the hon. member suggests? In some cases, Mr. Speaker, questioning is absolutely essential for crime detection. For example, with a murder or wounding among a youthful and riotous gang, any one of them could be suspect because there is no real motive; it was done in the heat of the moment. I suggest there is no way of solving that crime unless confession and questioning are usable. Without statements and confessions I suspect that 15 to 40 per cent of those now convicted would have escaped detection and conviction.
What would public reaction be in respect to sexual offences against young children if the offenders were not apprehended? Why are we so concerned about hampering the police? They are not a foreign power trying to harm our society; they are our representatives acting on our behalf in protecting society. I wonder if at times we have too much concern for the criminal and not enough for the good people who seek to be protected.
How does the proposed treatment of problem children compare with the treatment of other members of our society? I believe it is almost certain that we will allow the police to use wire-tapping to catch criminals. It just is not possible to do that without tapping the telephone lines of innocent people, which is a very serious invasion of privacy.
What about the breathalyzer? An accused can now be dragged out of his home, taken to a police station and asked to submit to a

breathalyzer test. He cannot have a lawyer present and he cannot refuse the test. If the reading is .09 he is convicted. He has a police record. Even if the magistrate believes that he had only one ounce of alcohol and was not impaired, he is still convicted and has a record.
I heard recently of a man in Cayuga being picked up. His reading was .09. He went to the next police station, which was in Hamilton, and they refused to give him the test. He then went to a hospital and asked for blood and urine tests but was refused. Many of these people have made only one mistake, yet we are giving this extreme authority to the police. I wonder why we are so conscious about criminals who may be repeaters and insist that they must have a lawyer present every time, and thus destroy the benefit of confession or statement evidence.
Although I cannot go so far as the hon. member has suggested, because I think it would amount to coddling criminals in comparison with the way in which we treat automobile drivers, I do have some concern for the poor and less experienced people who are brought to police stations. I would like to see a sign posted in all police stations which reads, "You need not give a statement." Perhaps it should go even further. The law could provide that one must sign a form to the effect that it was explained to him that he did not have to make a statement.

struck down. The accused is subject to questioning. The point of the lawyer being there is to prevent unfair questioning and abuse. The statement could be taken down. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the presentation of this bill by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) reflects, I think, the acute concern 21701-55
Canada Evidence Act
felt by society at the present time about the administration of justice and about justice itself. I stress this: I think our concern should be about justice, not only to the persons who are suspected of committing crimes but to all other members of society. I hope that never in this country will we be caught up in the kind of debate they have been conducting south of the border on the subject of law and order. Law and order can only truly be based upon justice and upon the realization by all people that their criminal law is administered in a just way.
The hon. member's proposal really falls into two parts. The first requires that any confession made by a person suspected of a crime must be voluntary. The second requires that before any confession made by a person suspected of a crime is admitted, it must be demonstrated that counsel was present at the interrogation and that he was able to consult counsel, unless the person suspected had clearly and unequivocally waived his right to counsel.
The law of this country has been for many years, and remains, that confessions made by a person accused of a crime can be admitted in evidence against him only if they are voluntary. We may, therefore, have cause to wonder whether it is necessary to incorporate this well known and well understood feature of our law into the Evidence Act. There may be good reason for not doing so if only because of the difficulties which might be created by statutory interpretation in the future denying to persons suspected of crimes the flexibility of approach which is inherent in the present application of this principle under the common law.
The principle has been asserted in many cases. One is the case of Boudreau v. The King, reported in 1949 Supreme Court Reports, page 262, at page 271. Mr. Justice Kellock, quoting the well known words of Lord Summer in Ibrahim v. The King, as follows:
It has long been established as a positive rule of English criminal law, that no statement by an accused is admissible in evidence against him unless it is shown by the prosecution to have been a voluntary statement, in the sense that it has not been obtained from him either by fear of prejudice or hope of advantage exercised or held out by a person in authority. The principle is as old as Lord Hale. The burden of proof in the matter has been decided by high authority.
It is clear from the jurisprudence and from the law as it is applied daily in the courts of

February 27, 1970
Canada Evidence Act
Canada that the burden of proof is on the Crown to establish that any confession made by an accused has been made voluntarily. In these circumstances, as many lawyers here know, a person accused of a crime is advised clearly of his right to remain silent; that any statement he has to make or might wish to make should not be influenced by any hope of advantage or fear of prejudice; and that any statement he might make can be used against him in subsequent proceedings.
There have been occasions in the past when it has been urged in the courts that the procedure for taking statements from accused should be codified in some sort of ritual. This suggestion has never been accepted by our courts. Mr. Justice Rand, in the case of Boudreau v. The King to which I have already referred, stated;
It would be a serious error to place the ordinary modes of investigation of crime in a straitjacket of artificial rules; and the true protection against improper interrogation or any kind of pressure or inducement is to leave the broad question to the court. Rigid formulas can be both meaningless to the weakling and absurd to the sophisticated or hardened criminal; and to introduce a new rite as an inflexible preliminary condition would serve no genuine interest of the accused and but add an unreal formalism to that vital branch of the administration of justice.
It appears to me the position as to voluntary statements being the only ones admissible in evidence against the accused is clearly established at the present time. It would add nothing to the law of Canada to include them in an amendment to the Evidence Act.
The other proposal in the bill would require as a condition of the admissibility of a statement that it be made in the presence of counsel unless the accused or suspected person has waived his right to counsel. This, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North has pointed out, arises from the decisions made in the United States Supreme Court, culminating in the cases of Escobedo v. Illinois, reported in 378 U.S. at page 478, and Miranda v. Arizona, 86 SCR, page 1602.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The effect of these decisions has been to invalidate confessions made by accused persons when their counsel was not present. What we are talking about here is the right of an accused person who has been taken to a police station to insist that a lawyer be present during his interrogation. This proposal raises very important issues, some of which have been referred to by the hon. member for

Peel South (Mr. Chappell). One of them is most certainly the availability of lawyers all over Canada who might be assumed to be readily on call at any time to attend a police station and remain there during the interrogation of accused persons.
Another problem that occurs to me is the difficulty of application of this procedure to particular offences. One that comes immediately to mind is that mentioned by the hon. member for Peel South-the important change which this Parliament made in the law last session permitting the use of breathalyzers for the detection of alcohol in accused persons and, further, making it an offence to refuse a breathalyzer test. It would appear to me that in this particular type of offence time is of the essence. The whole purport and intent of this important law would be lost if the proceedings were delayed while counsel was obtained.
Apart altogether from these considerations, it seems to me that we in this Parliament should not be too hasty in adopting a novel departure of this type in the law. We should recognize that the decisions of the United States Supreme Court have been the subject of much discussion in that country; indeed, they could be described as being greatly controversial. We must remember, in the words of one English judge, that "When a confession is well proved, it is the best evidence that can be produced".
The fact that the United States courts have ruled against the admissibility of confessions except when they were obtained in the presence of counsel has greatly disturbed public opinion in the United States. It is obvious from what one reads that not only law enforcement authorities but the public at large are concerned that people who really have voluntarily disclosed their connection with a crime are permitted to go free because counsel was not present in the police station at the time the confession was made. I believe that we in this Parliament should be very careful not to take steps to change the law and criminal procedure in a way that would not have wide acceptance by the majority of our fellow citizens.
Finally, I recognize, as others undoubtedly will, that the discussion in the United States does not run all one way. There are those who contend that the administration of justice there has not been unduly hampered by these new rules; that, indeed, the effect of these new rules has been to improve the quality of police work and crime detection. In my
February 27, 1970

submission, Mr. Speaker, it appears somewhat premature definitively to make a great change in our criminal law and procedure such as that envisaged in this bill without waiting a reasonable time to see how the new rules are in fact working out in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is undoubtedly aware of the fact that the Canadian Bill of Rights states affirmatively that a person is entitled to counsel. This has been interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada to mean that in any court proceeding an accused is entitled to have counsel.
I do not wish to infringe on the time, but in the course of his remarks my hon. friend referred to the offence of vagrancy, which is really poverty. This is a stated offence; it is not altogether a matter of procedure. He went on to say that he felt one person who had been accused might have done better had she had a lawyer. I should like to point out to my hon. friend that in Ontario, at any rate, under the present legal aid scheme duty counsel are now available in all magistrate's courts in the province and it is highly unlikely that a situation such as he described would happen again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right to make a confession or a statement to the police has two sides to it. Presumably, this motion purports to protect the rights of the individual. I am afraid that sometimes, if the motion were put into law, it might work against the rights of the individual. I think particularly of cases involving children and, again, I am relying on my own personal experience. Where an offence has been committed against a child, the child will usually blurt out the truth the first time he comes in contact with someone who he thinks will help him. But often there is pressure from the parents, guardians or other people who should have been responsible for the child in the first place, people who should have protected him, people who themselves may well 21701-55J
Canada Evidence Act
be responsible for the offence committed against the child, and in such cases it is very difficult to get to the truth of the matter.
Under British law, the burden of proving guilt is, of course, on the Crown. In many cases this burden on the Crown is a very onerous one indeed. It may be that in a case involving a child, the child himself is the only witness and the only possible proof of the crime is the statement of the child against the person who it is alleged has offended him. If any statutory hurdle is placed between the child and justice, I am sure that the hon. member who introduced the motion would be the first to say that it would be better to take a chance and leave things as they are. We have our courts and we have our judges. In every court I have been in the accused has been given the opportunity, if he thinks he is being treated injustly, to take the stand in his own defence. Certainly he has the right to speak, if not for himself then through a lawyer.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
As the last speaker said, in Ontario a man is entitled to seek legal advice if he needs it. In a great many cases I think a person is just as well off if he defends himself and he is clearly innocent. I have known cases where I believe that if the accused person had taken the stand he might have cleared himself, but by the time the case became tangled up with legal jargon, and so on, the court became confused. From my experience in court I am not sure that a voluntary statement has had any effect in causing injustice. The difficulty, of course, is where the statement is involuntary. However, that raises another aspect. I think a look might be taken at our legal system to see whether a little more protection might be given to people who are bullied.
In cases involving the arrest of juveniles I believe there should be an official of the court into whose custody the child could immediately be placed. This person should rarely be the police officer who makes the arrest. It should be a social worker or similar person. Perhaps a young person who is arrested should be treated in the way in which a female person is treated: in that case a matron takes charge of the accused person. In my opinion there is no reason why a matron or a social worker could not be called immediately and be at the police station when the child was brought in. If the child were

turned over to such a person immediately, there would be no possibility of anyone saying the child had been under duress. If any statement made by a child were considered to be inadmissible in court because the child did not go through the formality of calling legal counsel, I believe in many cases this would be to the detriment of the child himself and certainly to the detriment of the administration of justice.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what benefit there is in being the anchor man on a Friday afternoon. In any event, I would not want to proceed with my remarks this afternoon without first stating my profound admirat'on for the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow)-who has not had the benefit of or is otherwise not encumbered by a legal education-for bringing forth a bill which is so much involved with very difficult legal concepts.
I think I can express equal concern with him about the necessity of maintaining the standards of justice in Canada. I found that most of his observations were not directed in a sense to the question of the admissibility of confessions and statements, but to a large extent involved criticism of the courts in certain cases, or criticism of the police. In our society I do not believe there is any doubt that the public must always be watchful of the extent to which the police might abuse their powers, or the extent to which the courts might act against the true principles of justice.
With regard to the observation of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) about the breathalyzer test, I think that if he would review the debate which took place in the Justice Committee and this House he would find that the compulsory aspect of the breathalyzer test is quite different from the matter with which we are concerned today.
The bill before us is an attempt to curb police powers. It is an attempt to curb those powers by the introduction of the United States exclusionary rule of evidence which states that evidence illegally obtained cannot be admitted. We gave serious consideration to this rule during the hearings of the Committee on Justice when we were discussing the problems in respect of electronic surveillance.
I am diametrically opposed to the U.S. exclusionary rule being adopted in Canadian
IMr. Bigg.]
criminal jurisprudence. I am satisfied that our present rule, if properly applied, is the best available rule in this regard. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) quoted the rule. It has been quoted throughout the country for years in the famous words of Viscount Sumner. I do not intend to repeat what he said, but I have heard it quoted in courtrooms on many occasions when the learned judge has said that the principle is as old as Lord Hale.
Every time I hear that, I reflect on how old Lord Hale was at the time. In any event, in considering some aspects of the rule I think we should also consider what might be the result if this bill were passed. In the first instance, the history of the rule is founded upon centuries of experience in the British courts, that if a person who is about to be charged with a criminal offence-I think it should be noted that the real change in the law comes only after the man is in custody- is threatened by the policy with physical harm, or an inducement is held out to him by way of promise of favour, the concern of the courts is that what he says by way of confession might not be true because he would rather confess to a crime than suffer the physical harm to which he would be subjected.
I think it fair to state that many criminal lawyers today have grave doubts about the background and the substance of this rule; that is to say, that he would necessarily say things that were not true. But I think we should bear in mind the unpredictability of the human mind, the natural catharsis of confession, and the fact that people will often confess to crimes they have never committed whether they are threatened with regard to them or whether or not an inducement is held out.
Bearing all these matters in mind, I think the rule we have should be maintained without variation; if for no other reason, just as a matter of public policy to make certain we have some control over police powers when it comes to threatening an accused person or offering him promises of favour. I think it should principally be made clear that the rule applies solely to statements which are inculpatory. All of us who have practised in criminal courts have seen many people convicted as a result of making false statements which were not inculpatory but were later proven to be false.
